## About HexColor Pro - Who Builds These Color Tools

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/about

### About HexColor Pro

Maintained by Yao Xiangqian · Last updated November 11, 2026

HexColor Pro is an independent, free color toolkit for web designers and developers. It offers 13 browser-based tools for picking colors, generating CSS gradients and palettes, checking WCAG contrast, and converting between HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, and CMYK — plus a written guide and a blog on color theory and accessibility.

#### What is on this site

- 13 tools — color picker, gradient generator, contrast checker, palette generator, color schemes, converter, color names, shadow generator, random color, mixer, shades, temperature, and text color.

- A complete guide walking through every tool with worked examples.

- A blog covering color theory, WCAG accessibility, palettes, and design systems.

#### How the tools work

Every tool runs entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded: colors you enter are processed by JavaScript on your device, and no account is required to use any feature. The pages are static HTML served from a CDN, so they load fast and work the same on any modern browser.

HexColor Pro is free and supported by advertising. Ads never gate a tool and never change a computed result — the color math is plain JavaScript you can inspect in the page source.

#### Who builds it

HexColor Pro is built and maintained by Yao Xiangqian , an independent developer ( github.com/yxq1337 ). It started as a set of internal utility pages for everyday design work — checking a contrast pair, converting a hex value, building a quick gradient — and was published so other people could use them without a signup or a paywall.

Every tool is written and tested by the same person who writes the articles, so a claim on a blog page and the behavior of the tool on the adjacent page come from the same implementation. Questions, corrections, and tool requests go to the contact page .

#### Background

Yao Xiangqian is an independent developer who builds small, self-contained browser tools. Every tool on this site — the WCAG contrast math, the HEX/RGB/HSL/HSV/CMYK conversions, the mixing and ramp generation — is plain JavaScript written for that page, with no framework and no build step. The articles come from the same person, so a claim about how a ratio is computed can be checked against the code that computes it, one click away.

The work here is front-end — semantic HTML, plain CSS, and client-side JavaScript — and behind it sit ten years of design-system work: component libraries and color systems where a token that fails contrast is a bug, not a taste difference.

#### How the content is written and updated

The tool pages and articles are written by the maintainer. Where a claim depends on a standard, it cites the primary source — accessibility thresholds follow the W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 , published 5 October 2023, rather than secondary summaries. Articles show a publication date, and are revised when a cited standard or browser behavior changes.

If you spot an error, say which page and what is wrong; corrections are made on the page itself rather than in a reply, so the next reader sees the fix.

#### Using this site's content

You are welcome to quote or cite these pages with a link back. Machine-readable descriptions for AI agents are published at llms.txt and llms-full.txt .

## How to Use HexColor Pro — Complete Guide to All Tools

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/guide

### 📖 Complete Guide to HexColor Pro

Everything you need to know to get the most out of every color tool on this site.

##### 📋 Table of Contents

- 1 Color Picker

- 2 Color Converter

- 3 Gradient Generator

- 4 Contrast Checker

- 5 Palette Generator

- 6 Color Schemes

- 7 Color Names Finder

- 8 Shadow Generator

- 9 Keyboard Shortcuts

- ? FAQ

#### 🎨 1. Color Picker

The Color Picker is our flagship tool. It lets you explore any color in detail — see its hex, RGB, HSL, and CMYK values, plus a full palette of related colors.

##### How to use it:

- Click the color wheel or type a hex code (like #6366F1 ) in the input box.

- Use the sliders to fine-tune hue, saturation, and lightness.

- Scroll down to see automatically generated harmonies: complementary, analogous, triadic, and more.

- Click any color value to copy it to your clipboard.

- Use the shade/tint palette to find lighter or darker versions of the same color.

💡 Pro tip: Click the eyedropper icon (in supported browsers) to pick a color from anywhere on your screen — even from outside the browser window.

Open Color Picker →

#### 🔄 2. Color Converter

Convert between 8 different color formats instantly: HEX, RGB, HSL, CMYK, HSV, HWB, LAB, and XYZ.

##### How to use it:

- Enter a color value in any of the input fields — it doesn't matter which one.

- All other formats update automatically as you type.

- Click the copy button next to any value to copy it to your clipboard.

- Use the preview area to see how the color looks in context.

Supported formats: HEX, RGB, RGBA, HSL, HSLA, CMYK, HSV, HWB, LAB, XYZ

💡 Pro tip: You can paste any valid CSS color value — even named colors like rebeccapurple or tomato — and the converter will recognize it.

Open Color Converter →

#### 🌈 3. Gradient Generator

Create beautiful CSS gradients in seconds. Supports linear, radial, and conic gradients with up to 5 color stops.

##### How to use it:

- Choose a gradient type: Linear, Radial, or Conic.

- Add or remove color stops using the + and – buttons (2-5 stops supported).

- Click each color stop to change its color and position.

- Use the angle slider (for linear) or shape controls (for radial) to adjust the gradient direction.

- Click "Copy CSS" to copy the full gradient code to your clipboard.

- Try a preset from the gallery below to get started fast.

💡 Pro tip: For subtle, professional gradients, choose two colors that are close in hue — like blue to purple, or pink to orange. The closer the hues, the smoother the blend.

Open Gradient Generator →

#### 👁️ 4. Contrast Checker

Check if your text and background colors meet WCAG accessibility standards. Essential for making sure your website is usable by everyone.

##### How to use it:

- Enter a text color and a background color (or click to use the color picker).

- Instantly see the contrast ratio and pass/fail status for WCAG AA and AAA standards.

- Use the live preview to see how sample text looks with your color pair.

- Try the "auto-adjust" feature — we'll nudge the colors slightly to make them pass while staying as close as possible to your original.

WCAG standards at a glance:

- AA Normal: 4.5:1 minimum contrast for body text

- AA Large: 3:1 minimum for large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold+)

- AAA Normal: 7:1 minimum for enhanced accessibility

- AAA Large: 4.5:1 minimum for large text

💡 Pro tip: Contrast requirements are lower for large text because larger text is inherently easier to read. Text counts as "large" at 18pt (24px) or above, or 14pt (18.66px) bold or above.

Open Contrast Checker →

#### 🎯 5. Palette Generator

Generate beautiful, cohesive color palettes from a single base color. Perfect for finding a full design system palette in seconds.

##### How to use it:

- Enter a base color — this will be the "anchor" of your palette.

- Choose a palette style: Complementary, Analogous, Triadic, Split Complementary, Tetradic, Monochromatic, or Random.

- Your palette generates instantly. Click any color to copy its hex code.

- Use the shuffle button to generate variations.

- Export as CSS, SCSS, or JSON for use in your project.

💡 Pro tip: Start with a monochromatic palette for a clean, professional look. It's nearly impossible to make something that looks bad with a single hue.

Open Palette Generator →

#### ✨ 6. Color Schemes

Browse curated color schemes for different moods and use cases — from warm and energetic to calm and professional.

##### How to use it:

- Scroll through the categorized color scheme gallery.

- Click a category tag (Warm, Cool, Pastel, Dark, Vibrant, Minimal) to filter.

- Click any color in a scheme to copy its hex code.

- Use the "Apply to Palette" button to send a scheme to the Palette Generator for further customization.

Browse Color Schemes →

#### 📚 7. Color Names Finder

Find the name of any color. We match your color against a library of over 1,500 named colors to find the closest match.

##### How to use it:

- Enter a hex code or use the color picker to select a color.

- Instantly see the closest named color match, along with the color's hex, RGB, and HSL values.

- Scroll down to see similar named colors ranked by similarity.

- Click any color name to copy its hex code.

Our color name database includes:

- All 148 standard CSS/HTML named colors

- X11 color names

- Popular designer palette colors

- Pantone-inspired names

💡 Pro tip: Need to communicate a color to a client or teammate? Use the color name instead of the hex code — "dusty rose" is much easier to remember than "#D4869C."

Open Color Names →

#### 🌓 8. Shadow Generator

Create beautiful CSS box-shadows with a visual editor. Adjust blur, spread, distance, color, and opacity in real time.

##### How to use it:

- Use the sliders to adjust offset-X, offset-Y, blur radius, spread radius, and opacity.

- Choose a shadow color — try colored shadows for a modern look.

- Add multiple shadow layers for depth (click "Add Layer").

- See a live preview of the shadow on the demo card.

- Click "Copy CSS" to copy the full box-shadow code.

💡 Pro tip: For natural-looking shadows, use multiple layers: a soft, large shadow (far light) and a sharper, smaller shadow (near light). This mimics how real light works.

Open Shadow Generator →

#### ⌨️ 9. Tips & Shortcuts

All HexColor Pro tools support these common shortcuts and features:

- Click to copy: Click any hex, RGB, or HSL value to copy it to your clipboard.

- Color input: You can paste any valid CSS color — hex, rgb(), hsl(), or even color names.

- # is optional: When typing a hex code, you can skip the # symbol.

- 3-digit hex: Short hex codes like #f00 work everywhere.

- Dark mode: The site follows your system's dark mode preference automatically.

#### ❓ Frequently Asked Questions

##### Is HexColor Pro free to use?

Yes! All tools on HexColor Pro are completely free to use. There's no sign-up required and no hidden fees.

##### Do I need to install anything?

No. HexColor Pro runs entirely in your web browser. Just visit the site and start using the tools — no downloads, no plugins, no account needed.

##### Does HexColor Pro work offline?

Most of our tools work even if your internet connection drops, since all the color calculations happen in your browser. Just bookmark the page and you're good to go.

##### Are the colors accurate?

All color conversions use standard math formulas (sRGB color space). Your display will affect how colors look, but the values are mathematically correct.

##### Can I suggest a new tool?

Absolutely! We're always adding new tools. Use the contact page to send us your suggestions.

##### What browsers are supported?

All modern browsers: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, and Brave. Some advanced features (like the eyedropper tool) may only work in Chromium-based browsers.

## All 148 CSS Named Colors — Hex, RGB & HSL Reference | HexColor Pro

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/colors

### All 148 CSS named colors

CSS defines 148 named colors — keywords such as rebeccapurple, chartreuse, and lightgoldenrodyellow — each mapping to one exact sRGB value. Every entry below lists its hex code, RGB and HSL values, WCAG contrast on black and white, and a nine-step tint-and-shade ramp.

Grouped by hue. Names are case-insensitive in CSS: RebeccaPurple and rebeccapurple are the same color.

#### Light / white (23)

- Alice Blue #F0F8FF

- Azure #F0FFFF

- Beige #F5F5DC

## Embed the Contrast Checker — Free WCAG Widget | HexColor Pro

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/embed

### Embed the contrast checker

Drop a working WCAG contrast checker into any page with one iframe. No account, no tracking cookies, no ads, no build step — it is a static page that runs the contrast math in the visitor's browser.

#### Live preview

#### The embed code

```

Contrast checker by HexColor Pro

```

Copy embed code

#### How to use it

- Paste the snippet into a blog post, a design-system doc, or an accessibility checklist page.

- The widget is 420px wide at most and 300px tall; it scales down on mobile.

- Results update as the visitor types or picks a color — nothing is sent to a server.

- Keep the attribution line: it is the only condition for using the embed.

#### What it checks

The widget computes the WCAG 2.2 contrast ratio with the relative-luminance formula and reports the three thresholds that matter in practice: AA normal text (4.5:1), AA large text (3:1), and AAA normal text (7:1). For the full tool — with suggestions that reach a target ratio and a UI-component check — use the contrast checker .

## Privacy Policy - HexColor Pro

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/privacy

### Privacy Policy

Last updated: November 2026

#### Introduction

Welcome to HexColor Pro. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your information when you use our website.

#### Information We Collect

No Personal Data Collected Directly: HexColor Pro is a client-side color tool. All color calculations happen in your browser. We do not store or process any personal data on our servers.

Analytics & Advertising: We may use third-party services (such as Google Analytics, Google AdSense, or Ezoic) that collect anonymized usage data to improve the service and display relevant advertisements. These services may use cookies or similar technologies.

#### Cookies

We use localStorage in your browser to save your recent color history and preferences. This data never leaves your device. Third-party advertisers may also use cookies to serve ads based on your prior visits.

#### Third-Party Services

Our website may contain links to third-party websites. We have no control over and assume no responsibility for the content, privacy policies, or practices of any third-party sites or services.

#### Google AdSense / Ezoic

Google, as a third-party vendor, uses cookies to serve ads on our site. Google's use of the DART cookie enables it to serve ads based on your visit. You may opt out of the use of the DART cookie by visiting Google ad and content network privacy policy.

#### Your Rights

You have the right to access, correct, or delete your personal data. Since we do not store personal data on our servers, most of these rights are exercised directly through your browser settings or third-party service providers.

#### Changes to This Policy

We may update this privacy policy from time to time. We will notify you of any changes by posting the new policy on this page.

#### Contact Us

If you have any questions about this Privacy Policy, please contact us via our contact page .

## Color Picker - Free Online HEX, RGB, HSL Color Picker | HexColor Pro

#### How to Use the Color Picker

##### 🎯 What is a Color Picker?

A color picker is a tool that lets you select and identify colors. It's essential for designers, developers, and anyone working with digital color. Our color picker gives you every color format you need in real-time.

##### 📋 What Do the Color Formats Mean?

- HEX (#RRGGBB) — The most common format for web design. Six hexadecimal digits representing red, green, and blue channels.

- RGB (Red, Green, Blue) — Additive color model used in screens. Each value ranges from 0-255.

- HSL (Hue, Saturation, Lightness) — Human-friendly color model. Hue = color (0-360°), Saturation = intensity, Lightness = brightness.

- HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) — Similar to HSL but uses Value/brightness instead of lightness. Popular in design tools.

- CMYK (Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Key) — Subtractive color model used for print. Key = black.

##### 💡 Pro Tips

- Click any value to copy it to your clipboard instantly

- Your recent colors are saved automatically (in your browser)

- Use the palette generator to build full color schemes from one color

- Check contrast to make sure your text is accessible

##### 🔗 Related Tools

Check out our Gradient Generator , Contrast Checker , and Palette Generator to take your color work to the next level.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is a hex color code?

A hex code is a six-digit hexadecimal notation for an sRGB color, written #RRGGBB. Each pair runs from 00 to FF, so #FF0000 means red 255, green 0, blue 0. Three-digit shorthand such as #F00 expands to #FF0000.

##### How many colors can a color picker represent?

An 8-bit-per-channel picker covers 256 × 256 × 256 = 16,777,216 colors, usually written as 16.7 million. Adding an alpha channel multiplies that by 256 for transparency levels.

##### Should I use HEX or HSL in CSS?

Both are valid. HEX is compact and universally supported; HSL is easier to reason about when you need lighter, darker, or desaturated variants of one hue. Pick one convention per project and convert only when you need to share a value.

##### Why do the same HEX values look different on my phone?

Screens differ in gamma, white point, calibration, and brightness, so identical codes render differently. Check critical colors on a calibrated display, and never judge contrast by eye alone — measure the ratio instead.

#### How to Use CSS Gradients

##### 📐 Linear Gradients

The most common type. Colors transition along a straight line. Use the angle slider to rotate the direction.

- to right — left to right (equivalent to 90°)

- to bottom right — diagonal gradient

- 135deg — precise angle control

##### ⭕ Radial Gradients

Colors transition outward from a center point. Great for backgrounds, buttons, and spotlight effects.

##### 🎠 Conic Gradients

Colors transition around a center point (like a color wheel). Perfect for pie charts, color wheels, and creative effects.

##### 💡 Pro Tips

- Use 3-5 color stops for a rich, natural gradient

- Adjust stop positions to control where each color starts and ends

- Pair with the Color Picker to find the perfect starting colors

- Use subtle gradients (similar hues) for backgrounds, bold ones for accents

##### 🎯 More Tools

Try our Palette Generator to build full color schemes, or the Contrast Checker to ensure accessibility.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is the difference between linear, radial, and conic gradients?

Linear blends colors along a straight line at a set angle, radial blends outward from a center point, and conic sweeps colors around a center like a clock face. CSS exposes them as linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), and conic-gradient(), all supported in current browsers.

##### How many color stops should a gradient have?

Two stops are the minimum and stay predictable across browsers; three or four let you control the midpoint. Past about six stops a gradient starts to band on 8-bit displays, so add noise or interpolate in a wider color space instead of adding more stops.

##### Why does my gradient look banded?

Banding comes from 8-bit color steps: a slow transition between similar colors shows visible stripes. Shorten the transition distance, add a subtle noise overlay, or interpolate in a wider color space such as oklab with CSS color interpolation.

## Color Contrast Checker - WCAG Accessibility Test | HexColor Pro

The WCAG contrast ratio measures the luminance difference between text and its background on a scale from 1:1 to 21:1. WCAG 2.2 Level AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; Level AAA raises those thresholds to 7:1 and 4.5:1.

###### 💡 Suggested Fixes

Try these adjustments to pass AA:

#### Understanding WCAG Contrast Standards

##### 📏 What is Contrast Ratio?

Contrast ratio measures the difference in luminance between two colors. The scale ranges from 1:1 (same color) to 21:1 (black on white). Higher ratios mean easier readability.

##### 🏆 WCAG Levels Explained

- AA Normal — 4.5:1 minimum. Standard for body text (< 18pt / < 14pt bold).

- AA Large — 3:1 minimum. For large text (≥ 18pt / ≥ 14pt bold).

- AAA Normal — 7:1 minimum. Enhanced accessibility for body text.

- AAA Large — 4.5:1 minimum. Enhanced for large text.

##### 🔤 What Counts as "Large Text"?

WCAG defines large text as at least 18pt (24px) regular weight, or 14pt (18.66px) bold. If text is below that threshold, it falls under "Normal" requirements.

##### 💡 Pro Tips for Better Contrast

- Dark text on light backgrounds is generally more readable than the reverse

- Use the 60-30-10 rule: 60% dominant, 30% secondary, 10% accent color

- Test on actual screens — different displays vary in brightness and calibration

- Don't rely on color alone to convey information (e.g., use icons + color for status)

##### 🔗 Related Tools

Try the Palette Generator for harmonious color schemes, and the Color Picker to find perfect colors.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is a good contrast ratio for body text?

For body text, aim for at least 4.5:1, the WCAG 2.2 AA minimum for normal-size text. Many accessibility teams target 7:1 for long-form reading. A ratio of 3:1 is not enough for paragraph text — it only satisfies the large-text and UI-component rules.

##### Does a 4.5:1 ratio apply to buttons and borders?

No. Buttons, borders, icons, and other essential UI graphics fall under WCAG 1.4.11, which requires 3:1 against adjacent colors. The 4.5:1 requirement in 1.4.3 covers text; large text may use 3:1.

##### Is contrast ratio always the same as perceived readability?

Close, but not identical. The ratio uses relative luminance and ignores font weight, letter spacing, and ambient light. A 4.5:1 pair in a thin 12px typeface can read worse than a 4:1 pair in a heavy 20px one, so treat the minimum as a floor.

##### Why does black on white score 21:1 and not 100:1?

The scale is capped by the formula (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). With black at luminance 0 and white at 1, the result is 1.05 / 0.05 = 21. There is no higher value in WCAG, which is why 21:1 is the practical maximum.

##### Do transparency and opacity affect the ratio?

Yes. WCAG is evaluated on the final rendered colors, so a 60% opaque overlay over a background must be resolved to one solid color first. Blend the alpha channel over the layer beneath it, then test the resulting pair.

#### Color Harmony Modes Explained

##### 🔄 Complementary

Two colors opposite each other on the color wheel. Creates high contrast and vibrant combinations. Great for call-to-action buttons and accent elements.

##### 🌈 Analogous

Colors next to each other on the wheel. Creates harmonious, natural-feeling palettes. Perfect for backgrounds and cohesive designs.

##### 🔺 Triadic

Three colors evenly spaced on the wheel (120° apart). Balanced and vibrant with good contrast. Use one dominant, two accents.

##### ✂️ Split Complementary

A base color plus the two colors adjacent to its complement. Less tension than straight complementary, but still visually interesting.

##### 💎 Tetradic (Rectangle)

Four colors in two complementary pairs. Rich palette with lots of variety. Use one dominant, rest as accents.

##### ⚫ Monochromatic

Variations of a single hue (different lightness/saturation). Clean, elegant, and easy to get right. Great for minimalist designs.

##### ⚪ Shades

From light tint to dark shade of the same color. Useful for UI elements like buttons, cards, and text hierarchy.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What makes a color palette harmonious?

Harmony comes from a consistent relationship on the color wheel plus a deliberate contrast budget. Complementary, analogous, and triadic schemes each fix one kind of relationship; a usable palette then adds one accent and enough lightness separation for text and UI states.

##### How many colors should a website palette have?

Most production interfaces settle on five to seven: one or two neutrals for surfaces and text, one primary, one accent, and one or two semantic colors for success and error. A larger token set is fine, but the visible colors on one screen stay small.

##### What is the 60-30-10 rule?

It is a proportion guideline: 60% of the visual area in a dominant color, 30% in a secondary, 10% in an accent. It keeps a palette from feeling evenly weighted, and it maps cleanly onto CSS custom properties for background, surface, and accent.

## Color Scheme Generator - Color Palette Ideas | HexColor Pro

### Color Scheme Generator

#### Color Theory: The 6 Classic Schemes

##### 🌈 Analogous

Colors next to each other on the color wheel. Creates a harmonious, serene feel. Think sunsets, ocean blues, forest greens. Great for backgrounds and ambient designs.

##### ⚡ Complementary

Colors opposite each other on the wheel. High contrast, high energy. Think red-green, blue-orange, purple-yellow. Use sparingly for maximum impact — great for CTAs and highlights.

##### 🔺 Triadic

Three colors evenly spaced around the wheel (120° apart). Vibrant and balanced. The classic "primary colors" scheme is triadic. Good for playful, youthful designs.

##### 🎚️ Monochromatic

Variations of a single hue — different lightness and saturation. Super elegant and easy to get right. Perfect for minimalist designs, portfolios, and luxury brands.

##### 🔀 Split Complementary

A base color plus the two colors adjacent to its complement. Less intense than complementary but still has good contrast. Versatile and visually interesting.

##### 🔷 Tetradic (Double Complementary)

Four colors arranged as two complementary pairs. Rich with possibilities but trickier to balance. Best when one color is dominant and the rest support it.

##### 💡 Pro Tips for Using Color Schemes

- Follow the 60-30-10 rule: 60% dominant color, 30% secondary, 10% accent

- Start with the mood you want — calm? energetic? luxurious? — then pick a scheme

- Use neutral colors (white, gray, black) as your base, add color accents on top

- Always check accessibility — use our Contrast Checker tool to verify readability

- Less is more: start with 2-3 colors before adding more

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What are the classic color schemes?

Complementary (opposite on the wheel), analogous (adjacent), triadic (three colors evenly spaced), split-complementary (opposite plus its two neighbors), tetradic (two complementary pairs), and monochromatic (one hue at several lightness levels).

##### Which color scheme is best for a website?

Analogous and monochromatic schemes read as calm and are easiest to keep accessible; complementary and triadic give stronger contrast but need more discipline. Most sites use one dominant scheme plus a complementary accent rather than a pure scheme throughout.

##### Do color schemes work the same in dark mode?

No. Dark surfaces change perceived saturation and contrast: the same hue looks brighter against #0f172a than against white. Re-derive lightness for the dark theme and re-check contrast ratios instead of reusing the light-mode hex values.

HEX is a six-digit hexadecimal notation for sRGB color — #RRGGBB, where each pair runs from 00 to FF. RGB states the same color as three decimal channels, HSL restates it as hue, saturation, and lightness, and CMYK describes it for print. All four describe one color in different notations.

#### Color Formats Explained

##### 🎨 HEX

The most common web color format. Uses 6 hexadecimal digits (00-FF) for red, green, and blue. Example: #FF5733 . Used everywhere in web development — CSS, HTML, design tools.

##### 🔴 RGB

Red, Green, Blue — each from 0-255. Direct representation of how screens emit light. Example: rgb(255, 87, 51) . The standard for digital displays.

##### 🌀 HSL

Hue (0-360°), Saturation (%), Lightness (%). More intuitive for humans — "pick a hue, make it more/less saturated, lighter/darker." Great for creating color variations programmatically.

##### 💎 HSV

Hue, Saturation, Value (brightness). Similar to HSL but "value" goes from black to full color, while HSL lightness goes from black to white. Common in design software.

##### 🖨️ CMYK

Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Key (black). The print standard — based on ink absorption rather than light emission. Convert to CMYK when designing for print.

##### 💡 When to Use Which?

- Web / CSS → HEX or HSL (HEX for precision, HSL for easy tweaking)

- UI Design → HSL (easy to create consistent color systems)

- Print Design → CMYK (ensures accurate print output)

- Image Editing → RGB or HSV (full digital color range)

#### Frequently asked questions

##### Is HEX the same as RGB?

Yes — they are two encodings of the same sRGB value. #FF0000 and rgb(255, 0, 0) are identical, since hex FF is decimal 255. Converting between them is exact arithmetic with no color shift.

##### Why does CMYK look different from RGB?

CMYK is a subtractive ink model tied to a specific printer and paper, while RGB is an additive light model tied to a screen. A conversion gives a mathematical match, not a visual one, so proof print-critical colors against the actual press profile.

##### What is HSV used for if HSL exists?

HSV and HSL describe the same color family with different axes. HSV keeps full saturation at the top of its value axis, which suits pickers and scrubbing, while HSL's lightness axis maps more directly onto mixing a color with white or black in CSS.

##### Does converting HEX to HSL lose precision?

No. Both are three-channel encodings of the same sRGB value, so the conversion itself is lossless. Rounding only appears in the displayed numbers, which are usually shown as whole percentages for readability.

#### About Color Names

##### 🎨 Why Do Colors Have Names?

Color names help us communicate about colors precisely. While hex codes are exact, names are memorable and emotional — "coral" evokes a feeling that "#FF7F50" doesn't.

##### 📐 How Matching Works

We use the Delta E (ΔE) color difference formula in the Lab color space to find the closest named color to any hex input. A ΔE below 5 means the colors are nearly indistinguishable to the naked eye.

##### 📚 Where Names Come From

- Web Colors — the 148 CSS named colors with their exact hex, RGB, and HSL values

- X11 Colors — Extended color names from the X Window System

- Crayola & Pantone — Popular commercial color systems

- Natural Colors — Names inspired by nature (coral, olive, teal)

##### 💡 Pro Tips

- Use the color picker to experiment — the closest name updates in real time

- Looking for a specific vibe? Search "blue" or "pink" to see all shades

- Pair with the Palette Generator to build full schemes

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is the difference between a named color and a hex code?

A named color is a human label mapped to a specific value — CSS defines 148 keywords such as rebeccapurple and tomato. A hex code is the exact value. Names help communication; hex guarantees the color.

##### How does a color name finder pick the nearest name?

It converts both colors to a distance metric and returns the smallest. RGB distance is fast and common; perceptual spaces such as CIELAB or OKLab better match what the eye calls close, which matters for muted and dark colors.

##### Why does my hex code have no exact name?

Named colors cover a few hundred specific values out of the 16.7 million possible hex codes, so almost every code falls between two names. The nearest-name match is an approximation, not an identity.

## CSS Box Shadow Generator - Free Online Tool | HexColor Pro

### CSS Box Shadow Generator

Create beautiful, smooth shadows with live preview. Copy the CSS in one click.

A box-shadow generator builds the CSS box-shadow property from four parameters — offset X, offset Y, blur, and spread — plus a color. HexColor Pro previews the shadow live, including the inset variant, and copies the finished declaration in one click.

#### Understanding CSS Box Shadow

##### 📐 The Syntax

box-shadow: offset-x offset-y blur spread color inset;

- offset-x — Horizontal distance (positive = right, negative = left)

- offset-y — Vertical distance (positive = down, negative = up)

- blur — Softness of the shadow edge (0 = hard edge)

- spread — Size increase/decrease of the shadow

- color — Shadow color (use rgba for transparency)

- inset — Optional keyword for inner shadows

##### 🎯 Design Tips

- Use low opacity (10-30%) for natural-looking shadows

- Pair multiple shadows for realism: a soft one + a harder one

- Match shadow direction to your light source for consistency

- Lighter, larger shadows feel more "floating"; tight dark shadows feel "pressed"

- For dark mode, use colored shadows (match the element's hue) instead of black

##### ✨ Multiple Shadows

You can layer multiple shadows by comma-separating them. This creates more depth than a single shadow:

box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.05), 0 10px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.1), 0 20px 40px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What do the four box-shadow values mean?

offset-x and offset-y move the shadow, blur-radius softens its edge, and spread-radius grows or shrinks the shadow before blurring. Positive spread expands it, negative spread contracts it. An optional inset keyword draws the shadow inside the element.

##### Why does my CSS shadow look cheap?

Usually too much opacity and too little blur. Real light produces soft, low-contrast shadows: opacity around 0.08–0.15 with a large blur and a slight vertical offset reads as natural, while pure black at 0.5 reads as a sticker.

##### Can I layer multiple shadows?

Yes. box-shadow accepts a comma-separated list, and layering two or three shadows — a tight contact shadow plus a wide ambient one — is the usual way to get realistic elevation without filters.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### Is a random color generator truly random?

It uses the browser's pseudo-random number generator (Math.random or crypto.getRandomValues), which is unpredictable in practice but not suitable for secrets. For design work the difference does not matter.

##### What is the difference between a random color and a random palette?

A random color is one value drawn from the 16.7 million hex space, so it is usually saturated and rarely usable in UI. A random palette constrains hue, saturation, and lightness to keep the set coherent.

##### How do I reproduce a random color later?

You cannot reproduce a value drawn from an unseeded generator. If you need repeatability, record the hex code, or use a seeded generator so the same seed always yields the same sequence.

### Color Mixer

A color mixer blends two colors at a chosen ratio and reports the result. HexColor Pro interpolates channel by channel — a 50/50 mix lands halfway in RGB — and shows the intermediate steps, which makes it easy to build a smooth ramp between two brand colors.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### How is a color mix calculated?

By interpolating each channel: mixing two colors at 50% gives ((R1+R2)/2, (G1+G2)/2, (B1+B2)/2) for an RGB mix. Mixing in a perceptual space such as OKLab instead produces a result closer to how the blend appears to the eye.

##### Why does mixing two colors give a muddy result?

RGB mixing passes through desaturated midpoints, so mixing complementary hues lands near grey. That is a property of the color model, not a bug; add a third color, or mix in a perceptual space to keep chroma.

##### What is the difference between mixing light and mixing paint?

Light is additive: red plus green gives yellow. Paint is subtractive: red plus green gives a dark brown. Screens mix light, so an RGB mixer follows the additive rule.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is the difference between tints, shades, and tones?

A tint mixes the base color with white, a shade mixes it with black, and a tone mixes it with grey. Tints step toward pastel, shades toward deep and dark, tones toward muted.

##### How many steps should a color ramp have?

Ten steps is the usual default because it maps cleanly onto 50–900 token naming. Fewer than five gives too little control over hover and disabled states; more than twelve rarely earns its maintenance cost.

##### Should a shade ramp be linear in lightness?

Not necessarily. Linear mixing in sRGB compresses perceived lightness at the dark end, so many design systems space the steps perceptually using OKLCH or HSL lightness, so that 500 and 600 look evenly separated.

Color temperature converts a Kelvin value into an RGB or HEX color, based on the light a black body emits at that temperature: roughly 1,000K reads as candlelight, 6,500K as daylight, and 10,000K as clear blue sky. HexColor Pro maps Kelvin to hex for lighting and UI references.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What does color temperature measure?

It describes the color of light on the Kelvin scale, from about 1,800K for candlelight through 6,500K for daylight to over 10,000K for clear sky. Lower values read warm and orange, higher values cool and blue.

##### Why does 6,500K look different on my screen than in a photo?

Camera white balance, display calibration, and surrounding colors all shift perception. The Kelvin value describes the light source objectively; it does not guarantee how a particular screen renders it.

##### How do I use color temperature in UI design?

Use warm tints for calm, ambient surfaces and cool tints for technical or focus-heavy ones, and keep the shift consistent across a theme. Re-check contrast after shifting temperature, since luminance changes with it.

##### Auto Text Color Generator

#### Frequently asked questions

##### How do I choose the best text color for a background?

Pick the candidate that maximizes contrast ratio: black text on light backgrounds, white on dark, computed with the WCAG relative-luminance formula. Then verify the ratio clears 4.5:1 for body text rather than trusting the choice by eye.

##### Is black or white always the best choice?

No. Near-black (#111827) and near-white (#f8fafc) usually read softer than the pure values and avoid the harsh edge pure black and white produce on large text areas. Both still need a measured contrast check.

##### What about text over images or gradients?

Contrast is judged against the worst-case pixel behind each glyph. Add a scrim or solid overlay, or test the lightest and darkest regions separately; a single average value hides the failures.

## WCAG Contrast Ratio Explained: How to Check & Fix Color Accessibility | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/wcag-contrast-ratio-guide

### WCAG Contrast Ratio Explained: How to Check & Fix Color Accessibility

Complete guide to WCAG 2.2 contrast ratios, AA vs AAA standards, how to measure contrast, and common mistakes that make your site inaccessible.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 8, 2026 · 1900 words · 8 min read

#### What Is WCAG and Why Does It Matter?

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are a set of recommendations for making web content accessible to people with disabilities. Published by the W3C, they're the global standard for digital accessibility.

Color contrast is one of the most basic — and most commonly violated — accessibility requirements. An estimated 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency. Poor contrast doesn't just affect them: it affects everyone using your site in bright sunlight, on low-brightness screens, or at small font sizes.

📊 Legal note: WCAG 2.1 AA is the legal standard in the EU (EN 301 549), the US (for federal and many state websites under ADA), Canada, Australia, and many other countries. Failing contrast can lead to lawsuits.

#### WCAG Contrast Ratio Standards: AA vs AAA

WCAG 2.2 defines two compliance levels for text contrast:

| Level | Normal Text | Large Text | Required For |

| AA | 4.5:1 minimum | 3:1 minimum | Most legal requirements |

| AAA | 7:1 minimum | 4.5:1 minimum | Highest standard, recommended |

"Large text" is defined as at least 18pt (24px) bold or 24pt (32px) regular weight. Icons and UI components like form borders or checkboxes also need a 3:1 contrast ratio against their background under WCAG 2.2.

#### How Contrast Ratio Is Calculated

The contrast ratio is calculated using the relative luminance of two colors. Luminance is not the same as brightness — it's the perceived brightness of a color, weighted according to how the human eye responds to different wavelengths.

The formula uses the sRGB color space and weights green the most (since our eyes are most sensitive to green light), red medium, and blue the least:

Luminance = 0.2126 × R + 0.7152 × G + 0.0722 × B

Where R, G, and B are gamma-corrected values from 0 to 1 (not the raw 0-255 values). The contrast ratio is then:

(L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)

Where L1 is the lighter color's luminance and L2 is the darker one's. The 0.05 accounts for flare in real-world viewing conditions.

#### What Counts as "Text" Under WCAG?

Not every text element needs to meet the contrast standard. Here are the exceptions:

- Logos: Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement.

- Incidental text: Text in inactive UI components, or text that is purely decorative and not interacted with.

- Placeholder text: Form field placeholders are exempt, but it's still good practice to make them readable.

- Disabled controls: Buttons or inputs in a disabled state.

That said, the exceptions are narrow. All body text, headings, navigation links, form labels, and button text must meet the minimum contrast.

#### 5 Common Contrast Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)

##### 1. Low-contrast placeholder text

Many designers use light gray placeholders that fail 4.5:1. While technically exempt, users with low vision can't read them. Fix: Use a medium gray with at least 3:1 contrast.

##### 2. Colored text on colored backgrounds

Yellow text on white, or light blue on dark blue — both look fine in design software but fail in practice. Always check with a contrast checker.

##### 3. Text over images or gradients

White text on a hero image might pass in the center but fail near light areas. Fix: Add a semi-transparent overlay or text shadow to ensure consistent contrast.

##### 4. Thin font at small sizes

A 14px light font weight might technically pass 4.5:1 but still be hard to read. Consider AAA (7:1) for body text to add visual buffer.

##### 5. Disregarding color blindness

Contrast ratio alone doesn't guarantee colorblind accessibility. Red-green combinations might have good contrast but be indistinguishable to 8% of men. Always check with a color blindness simulator.

⚠️ Don't rely on your eyes: What "looks readable" is often wrong. Human eyes adapt and compensate, so you can't judge contrast by eye alone. Always use a tool.

#### How to Check Contrast on Your Website

There are several ways to audit your site's contrast:

- Our Color Contrast Checker : Paste your foreground and background hex codes. Instantly see if you pass AA and AAA, with WCAG 2.2 validation.

- Browser DevTools: In Chrome DevTools, inspect any text element and look for the "Contrast" line in the color picker. It shows the ratio and pass/fail.

- Lighthouse: Google's Lighthouse audit (in DevTools → Lighthouse tab) scans all text contrast on a page.

- axe DevTools: A browser extension that does comprehensive accessibility audits, including contrast.

#### The Difference Between WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 for Contrast

WCAG 2.2 (published in October 2023) added one new success criterion related to visual appearance: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) at level AA. It requires that focus indicators aren't completely hidden by other content — not directly a contrast issue, but related to visibility.

For contrast ratios specifically, WCAG 2.2 keeps the same AA and AAA thresholds as 2.0 and 2.1. The standards are stable; what changes is how we test for them and what UI elements they apply to.

#### Practical Tips for Better Contrast

- Design with contrast first, not last: Build your color palette to meet standards from the start, rather than fixing issues at the end.

- Use 8-point tints and shades: A systematic palette (like Tailwind's 50-950 scale) ensures you always have accessible options.

- Test both themes: If you have light and dark mode, test contrast for both — dark mode is not automatically more accessible.

- Check edge cases: Error states, success messages, disabled buttons, and link colors all need contrast checks.

#### Start Testing Now

Ready to check if your colors are accessible? Use our free Color Contrast Checker — it takes two seconds, gives you instant WCAG 2.2 AA/AAA results, and even suggests adjustments if your colors fail.

## Hex to RGB: The Complete Conversion Guide (With Examples) | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/hex-to-rgb-conversion-guide

### Hex to RGB: The Complete Conversion Guide (With Examples)

Learn how to convert hex color codes to RGB manually or with a calculator. Includes formula, examples, and a free online converter tool.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 8, 2026 · 1800 words · 8 min read

#### What Is a Hex Color Code?

A hex color code is a six-character (plus an optional two for alpha) representation of a color using the hexadecimal numbering system. It always starts with a # symbol followed by six characters from 0-9 and A-F .

The six characters are split into three pairs: RR for red, GG for green, and BB for blue. Each pair represents a value from 0 to 255 — exactly matching RGB channels.

For example, #FF0000 means full red (255), no green (0), and no blue (0) — pure red.

💡 Quick fact: Hex codes are case-insensitive. #FF0000 and #ff0000 are identical. Most designers use uppercase for readability.

#### The Hex to RGB Formula

Converting hex to RGB is straightforward once you know how base-16 works. Here's the step-by-step formula:

- Take the six-digit hex code and remove the #

- Split it into three pairs: first two = red, middle two = green, last two = blue

- For each pair, convert the hexadecimal value to a decimal number from 0-255

The hex-to-decimal conversion works like this: each position represents 16 raised to a power. The left character is the "16s place" (16 1 ) and the right character is the "1s place" (16 0 ).

For pair FF : F (15) × 16 + F (15) × 1 = 240 + 15 = 255

For pair 80 : 8 × 16 + 0 × 1 = 128 + 0 = 128

#### Example 1: Convert #2563EB to RGB

Let's walk through a real example — the indigo blue used in many modern designs.

| Component | Hex Pair | Calculation | Decimal Value |

| Red | 25 | 2 × 16 + 5 = 37 | 37 |

| Green | 63 | 6 × 16 + 3 = 99 | 99 |

| Blue | EB | 14 × 16 + 11 = 235 | 235 |

Result: rgb(37, 99, 235) — which is Tailwind's blue-600.

#### Example 2: Convert #10B981 to RGB

An emerald green, common in success states and fintech designs.

| Component | Hex Pair | Calculation | Decimal Value |

| Red | 10 | 1 × 16 + 0 = 16 | 16 |

| Green | B9 | 11 × 16 + 9 = 185 | 185 |

| Blue | 81 | 8 × 16 + 1 = 129 | 129 |

Result: rgb(16, 185, 129) — the famous emerald-500.

#### What About 3-Digit Hex Codes?

You'll sometimes see shorthand hex codes like #F00 for red or #0AF for blue. These are valid in CSS and work by doubling each character.

#F00 → #FF0000 → rgb(255, 0, 0)

#0AF → #00AAFF → rgb(0, 170, 255)

Shorthand hex only works when both characters in each pair are identical. It's mainly used for saving bytes in CSS.

#### 8-Digit Hex: Adding Transparency

Modern CSS supports 8-digit hex codes where the last two digits represent the alpha (transparency) channel. The same conversion applies:

#FF000080 → red: FF (255), green: 00 (0), blue: 00 (0), alpha: 80 (128/255 ≈ 50% opacity)

The alpha value 00 means fully transparent, and FF means fully opaque. This is equivalent to rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5) .

⚠️ Browser support: 8-digit hex codes work in all modern browsers (Chrome 62+, Firefox 52+, Safari 10+). For older browser support, use rgba() instead.

#### Fastest Way to Convert Hex to RGB

Doing the math by hand is fine for understanding, but in practice you'll want a faster method. Here are three options:

- Online converter tool: Use our Color Converter — paste your hex code and instantly get RGB, HSL, HSV, and CMYK values.

- Browser DevTools: In Chrome DevTools, click any color swatch in the Styles panel to toggle between hex, rgb, and hsl formats.

- Design software: Figma, Sketch, and Photoshop all show hex and RGB side by side in the color picker.

#### Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Confusing the pair order: Hex is always RR-GG-BB, never any other order.

- Forgetting case insensitivity: #abcdef and #ABCDEF are the same color.

- Adding spaces: Hex codes have no spaces. #FF 00 00 is invalid.

- Using 4-digit hex for opacity: #F008 = 50% red, but only works if you know the shorthand rule.

#### Next Steps

Now that you understand hex to RGB conversion, you might want to explore other color models. Head over to our Color Converter to try converting between 7 different color formats instantly.

## What Is HSL Color? A Beginner's Guide to Hue, Saturation & Lightness | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/what-is-hsl-color

### What Is HSL Color? A Beginner's Guide to Hue, Saturation & Lightness

Understand the HSL color model, how it differs from RGB and HEX, and why designers love it for creating consistent color systems.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 8, 2026 · 1700 words · 8 min read

#### What Does HSL Stand For?

HSL stands for Hue, Saturation, and Lightness . It's a color model that describes colors in a way that's much more intuitive for humans than RGB or hex codes.

While RGB describes a color as "how much red, green, and blue light," HSL describes it as "what color, how vivid, and how bright." It's a cylindrical representation where each dimension maps to something you can name.

#### The Three Components of HSL

##### Hue (0° – 360°)

Hue is the base color, represented as an angle on the color wheel. 0° is red, 120° is green, 240° is blue, and 360° wraps back to red. Every number in between is a different hue — 30° is orange, 270° is purple, 180° is cyan, and so on.

Because hue is circular, 350° and 10° are neighbors (both red-ish), even though numerically they're far apart. This is what makes HSL so useful for creating harmonious palettes.

##### Saturation (0% – 100%)

Saturation is how "colorful" or vivid the color is. 0% saturation gives you pure gray — no color at all. 100% is the most intense, fully saturated version of that hue. Everything in between is progressively more muted.

Designers often work in the 30-70% saturation range for UI elements. Fully saturated colors (100%) can be harsh on the eyes and difficult to pair with others.

##### Lightness (0% – 100%)

Lightness is how bright the color is. 0% lightness is always black, regardless of hue or saturation. 100% is always white. 50% is the "pure" color — neither darkened nor lightened.

Wait — if lightness is 50%, is the color always the same brightness? Not exactly. A 50% lightness yellow looks brighter than a 50% lightness blue because our eyes perceive yellow as brighter. Lightness is a mathematical property, not a perceptual one. (If you want perceptual lightness, look into the LCH color model.)

🎯 Pro tip: Want to make a color darker or lighter but keep the exact same hue? Just adjust the L value. That's why HSL is perfect for creating tint/shade scales — you don't have to recalculate anything.

#### HSL vs RGB vs Hex: Which Should You Use?

| Model | Best For | Example | Human Readable? |

| Hex | Copy-pasting, CSS | #6366f1 | No |

| RGB | Screen rendering | rgb(99, 102, 241) | No |

| HSL | Design, palettes, systems | hsl(239, 84%, 67%) | Yes |

| HSL / HSV | Artistic control | hsv(239, 59%, 95%) | Yes |

For day-to-day web work, most designers use hex codes in their CSS but think in HSL when building palettes. Modern CSS lets you use any format — and HSL custom properties are increasingly popular for design systems.

#### Why Designers Love HSL

##### 1. It makes palettes trivial

Want a monochromatic palette? Keep H and S constant, vary L from 10% to 90%. Want analogous colors? Keep S and L constant, rotate H by ±30°. Want complementary? Add 180° to H. It's that simple.

##### 2. It's the easiest way to tweak brightness

In hex or RGB, making a color 10% darker involves recalculating all three channels. In HSL, you just subtract 10 from L. Done.

##### 3. It maps to how we talk about color

When someone says "that blue is too bright," they're talking about lightness. "Make it less intense" means lower saturation. "Shift it toward teal" means adjust hue. HSL aligns with natural language in a way RGB never will.

#### How to Convert HSL to RGB

While you'll usually use a tool for this, it's useful to understand the math. The HSL to RGB conversion is more complex than hex↔RGB because it involves trigonometric-looking steps:

- If saturation is 0%, the color is gray — R, G, B all equal lightness.

- Otherwise, calculate temporary values based on lightness and saturation.

- For each of R, G, B, determine which sector of the hue wheel it's in and compute accordingly.

The full algorithm is a bit lengthy to show here. Unless you're writing a color library, just use our Color Converter — it does HSL ↔ RGB ↔ hex and 6 other formats instantly.

#### HSL in CSS: Practical Examples

HSL works in all modern browsers and is great for design systems with CSS variables:

``` :root { --brand-h: 239; --brand-s: 84%; --brand-l: 67%; --brand: hsl(var(--brand-h) var(--brand-s) var(--brand-l)); --brand-dark: hsl(var(--brand-h) var(--brand-s) calc(var(--brand-l) - 15%)); --brand-light: hsl(var(--brand-h) var(--brand-s) calc(var(--brand-l) + 15%)); } ```

With this setup, changing your entire brand color is as simple as changing one number ( --brand-h ). All the light and dark variants update automatically.

#### HSV vs HSL: What's the Difference?

You'll also see HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) in design tools. They're similar but not identical:

- HSL's "lightness" 100% = white , 0% = black, 50% = pure color

- HSV's "value" 100% = pure color , 0% = black. White is achieved by lowering saturation to 0%.

- HSV is what Photoshop, Figma, and most design tools use in their color pickers.

- HSL is what CSS supports natively.

💡 Confused yet? Don't worry — you rarely need to think about the difference. Our Color Converter shows you HSL, HSV, RGB, hex, and more all on one screen.

#### Start Experimenting

The best way to understand HSL is to play with it. Open our Color Picker , switch to HSL mode, and drag the sliders around. Notice how hue rotates the color wheel, saturation controls intensity, and lightness slides from black to white.

## How Many Hex Colors Are There? (And Why It's Not Exactly 16 Million) | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/how-many-hex-colors-are-there

### How Many Hex Colors Are There? (And Why It's Not Exactly 16 Million)

The real answer to how many hex color codes exist, including transparency channels, named colors, and the human eye's real perception limit.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 8, 2026 · 1500 words · 8 min read

#### The Short Answer

There are 16,777,216 possible hex color codes in the standard 6-digit format. That's 256 shades of red × 256 shades of green × 256 shades of blue = 256³ = 16,777,216 unique combinations.

But the full answer is more interesting than that. Let's break it down.

#### Where 16.7 Million Comes From

A 6-digit hex code represents 3 bytes of data — one byte each for red, green, and blue. One byte = 8 bits = 256 possible values (0-255).

| Channel | Hex Range | Decimal Range | Values |

| Red (RR) | 00 – FF | 0 – 255 | 256 |

| Green (GG) | 00 – FF | 0 – 255 | 256 |

| Blue (BB) | 00 – FF | 0 – 255 | 256 |

| Total | | 16,777,216 |

256 × 256 × 256 = 2 24 = 16,777,216. This is also called "24-bit color" or "True Color."

#### What About 8-Digit Hex? 4.3 Billion More

With 8-digit hex codes (which add an alpha/transparency channel), you get one more byte:

256 × 256 × 256 × 256 = 2 32 = 4,294,967,296 possible combinations

That's over 4 billion — roughly half the population of Earth. But most of those are just different transparency levels of the same 16.7 million colors. So it's technically correct but a bit misleading to say "4 billion colors."

#### 3-Digit Hex: Only 4,096 Colors

The shorthand 3-digit format ( #RGB ) has far fewer:

16 × 16 × 16 = 16³ = 4,096 colors

That's because each digit can only be 0-F (16 values) instead of two digits (256 values). 4,096 colors was the standard for "high color" displays in the early 2000s. Today it's mainly used for CSS brevity.

🤓 Nerd fact: Named web colors? There are only 140 of them defined in the CSS color specification. That's 140 out of 16.7 million — 0.0008%. The vast majority of hex colors have no name at all.

#### But How Many Colors Can Humans Actually See?

Here's where it gets philosophical. 16.7 million sounds like a lot, but can we actually tell them all apart?

The answer depends on who you ask and how you measure. Most studies put the number of distinguishable colors between:

- ~1 million — conservative estimate for color differences under ideal conditions

- ~10 million — more commonly cited figure for total distinguishable colors

- Up to 100 million — claimed by some studies for people with tetrachromacy (4 cone types instead of 3)

So 16.7 million is probably more than most people can distinguish — but not by as much as you might think. And there are definitely many real-world colors that 8-bit sRGB can't represent accurately.

#### Why 16.7 Million Isn't Enough

You might think 16.7 million colors is overkill. It's not. Here's why:

##### Smooth gradients need them

A gradient from dark blue to light blue across a 1920-pixel-wide screen needs ~1920 distinct shades to look smooth. With only 256 shades per channel, you can start to see visible banding in gradients — especially in dark areas where our eyes are more sensitive to differences.

##### Color correction and editing

When you adjust brightness, contrast, or apply filters, you're stretching and compressing the available color values. Starting with only 256 levels per channel means you'll see posterization (banding) after just a couple of adjustments. That's why professional photo editing uses 16-bit per channel (65,536 levels) or even 32-bit floating point.

##### Gamut limitations

sRGB (what hex codes describe) only covers about 35% of visible colors. Wider gamuts like Display P3 or Rec. 2020 can show more vivid colors that hex/sRGB literally cannot represent. That's why modern devices are moving to P3 displays and CSS color(display-p3 ...) syntax.

#### Hex Colors in Practice

Even though 16.7 million sounds vast, designers and developers end up using a surprisingly small subset. A typical app or website might use only 50-200 distinct colors across its entire design system. The rest of the 16.7 million are unused — but having them available means you always have the exact shade you need.

Want to explore the space? Our Color Picker lets you click anywhere on the full 16.7 million color spectrum and instantly get the hex code.

#### Fun Hex Color Facts

- #000000 (black) and #FFFFFF (white) are the most commonly used hex colors in CSS — no surprise.

- The most "average" color — #808080 — is literally middle gray in every channel.

- In hexadecimal, A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. That's why FF = 255 (15×16+15).

- "Hex" comes from the Greek word "hexa" meaning six — referring to the six characters in a standard hex color code.

#### Wrapping Up

So how many hex colors are there? 16,777,216 for standard 6-digit codes, plus a lot more if you count alpha. But the real answer is: enough for everyday web design, but not enough for everything. The future is wider color gamuts and higher bit depths — but hex isn't going anywhere anytime soon.

## What Color Is #FF0000? Understanding Hex Color Codes | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/what-color-is-ff0000

### What Color Is #FF0000? Understanding Hex Color Codes

Deep dive into the world's most famous hex code. Learn how hex colors work, the structure of a hex code, and why red is FF0000.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 8, 2026 · 1600 words · 8 min read

#### The Quick Answer

#FF0000 is pure red . It's the brightest, most saturated red you can display in a standard hex color code — 255 red, 0 green, 0 blue.

You've seen it a million times. But have you ever stopped to wonder why it's "FF" and not something else? Or why it's the most famous hex code in the world?

#### Breaking Down #FF0000

Every 6-digit hex color code follows the format #RRGGBB — two characters for red, two for green, two for blue. Let's split #FF0000 apart:

| Channel | Hex Value | Decimal Value | Meaning |

| Red (RR) | FF | 255 | Maximum red |

| Green (GG) | 00 | 0 | No green |

| Blue (BB) | 00 | 0 | No blue |

FF in hexadecimal equals 255 in decimal. That's the maximum value a single byte can hold — which is why it's the "fullest" red possible in 24-bit color.

#### Why Hexadecimal? Why Not Decimal?

You might be wondering why we use hex at all. Why not just write rgb(255, 0, 0) and be done with it?

There are a few historical and practical reasons:

- Compact: 6 characters vs "rgb(255, 0, 0)" — shorter is better when you're writing thousands of colors in CSS.

- Binary-friendly: Each hex digit = 4 bits. Two digits = 8 bits = 1 byte. It's a perfect fit for how computers store color data.

- Early web tradition: Hex colors were used in the first versions of HTML and CSS, and the tradition stuck.

- Copy-paste friendly: It's a single token — no commas, no spaces, no function syntax.

💡 Conversion trick: To convert a hex pair to decimal in your head: first digit × 16 + second digit. For FF: 15 × 16 + 15 = 255. That's it.

#### Shades of #FF0000

Pure red is bright — sometimes too bright. Here's a scale of reds going from pure red down to near-black, all just different lightness levels of the same hue:

| Hex | RGB | Name / Description |

| #FF6666 | 255, 102, 102 | Light red / coral red |

| #FF3333 | 255, 51, 51 | Bright red |

| #FF0000 | 255, 0, 0 | Pure red (the classic) |

| #CC0000 | 204, 0, 0 | Dark red / ruby |

| #990000 | 153, 0, 0 | Deep red / burgundy |

| #660000 | 102, 0, 0 | Very dark red / maroon |

| #330000 | 51, 0, 0 | Nearly black red |

Want to generate your own scale? Use our Color Shades Generator — just paste #FF0000 and you get 10 shades instantly.

#### The History of Red in Digital Design

Red has always been special in computing. Here's why:

##### The first color displays

Early computers didn't have color at all — they had monochrome displays, usually green or amber phosphor. When color arrived in the 1970s and 80s, it often came in the form of RGB monitors — and red was always the "first" channel.

##### HTML and the birth of the web

In the early web (HTML 3.2, 1997), you could use 16 named colors. Red was one of them. The hex code #FF0000 was everywhere — links, error messages, emphasis. It was the web's first "attention" color.

##### Red in UI design today

Red still means "stop," "error," "danger," and "delete" in almost every interface. It's the most emotionally intense color — which is why you should use it sparingly. Too much red causes stress and alarm fatigue.

#### What Makes #FF0000 Special

- It's one of the 16 original named web colors (just red in CSS).

- It has the shortest 3-digit hex shorthand: #F00 (double each digit → #FF0000).

- It's the purest primary color in the RGB model — no mixing of other channels.

- It's used in everything from stop signs to error messages to YouTube's logo.

- Red is the first color babies can see (after black and white).

#### Colors That Go With #FF0000

Pure red is powerful and hard to pair. Here are 5 color schemes that work:

##### 1. Classic Red + Black

Red on black. Think Ferrari, Coca-Cola, or a deck of cards. High contrast, bold, classic. But use sparingly — it can feel aggressive.

##### 2. Red + Cream

Red with warm off-white ( #FFF8E7 ). Softer than red on white, feels vintage and premium. Great for editorial and fashion.

##### 3. Red + Navy

Red with deep navy blue ( #0F2B5B ). Nautical, patriotic, trustworthy. The classic Americana palette.

##### 4. Red + Teal

Red with teal ( #14B8A6 ). Modern and bold — complementary colors that pop without being cliché. Popular in startup branding.

##### 5. Red + Gray Scale

Red on a neutral gray background. The safe choice for dashboards and apps. Red signals errors and alerts; everything else is gray.

⚠️ Accessibility warning: Pure red (#FF0000) on white has a contrast ratio of only 3.99:1 — below the WCAG AA standard of 4.5:1 for body text. Use a darker red like #CC0000 or #D32F2F for text.

#### Red Around the World

Red carries different cultural meanings — something to consider if you're designing for a global audience:

- China & East Asia: Red is lucky, prosperous, and celebratory. It's the color of Chinese New Year and weddings.

- Western cultures: Red means danger, stop, love, and passion. It's also associated with communism and revolution.

- India: Red represents purity, marriage, and fertility. Brides traditionally wear red.

- South Africa: Red is associated with mourning.

#### Explore More Colors

Now that you know everything about #FF0000, why not explore the other 16,777,215 colors? Use our Color Picker to find the perfect shade, or the Color Converter to translate between hex, RGB, HSL, and more.

## CMYK to RGB: Why Colors Look Different on Screen vs Print | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/cmyk-to-rgb-difference

### CMYK to RGB: Why Colors Look Different on Screen vs Print

Understand the difference between additive and subtractive color, why printed colors never match screens, and how to convert CMYK to RGB correctly.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 8, 2026 · 1700 words · 8 min read

#### Why CMYK and RGB Are Different

Have you ever designed something on screen that looked perfect, then printed it and thought — "why does this look so dull and different?" You're not imagining it. Screen colors and printed colors are fundamentally different things, and understanding why will save you a lot of frustration.

The core difference comes down to additive vs subtractive color mixing — two completely different physical processes that produce color in opposite ways.

#### RGB: Additive Color (Light)

RGB (Red, Green, Blue) is how screens produce color. It's called "additive" because you start with black (no light) and add colored light on top of it.

- Add all three colors at full intensity → white

- No light at all → black

- Different combinations make the 16.7 million colors we see on screen

Every screen — your phone, monitor, TV, even smartwatch — uses tiny red, green, and blue subpixels that emit light. When you look at a screen, you're looking directly at light sources.

#### CMYK: Subtractive Color (Ink)

CMYK (Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Key/Black) is how printing produces color. It's called "subtractive" because you start with white (the paper) and subtract light by printing ink on top of it.

- Ink absorbs (subtracts) certain wavelengths of light

- The light that isn't absorbed bounces back to your eye — that's the color you see

- Cyan ink absorbs red light, magenta absorbs green, yellow absorbs blue

- Add all three and you should get black — but in practice you get a muddy brown, so printers add a pure black ink (the K in CMYK)

When you look at a printed page, you're looking at reflected ambient light — not a light source itself.

💡 Why K for black? Because B already means Blue in RGB, so the printing industry uses K for "Key plate" — the black plate that adds detail and contrast. It's also sometimes said to stand for the last letter of "blacK."

#### The Gamut Problem: Why They Never Match

"Gamut" is the range of colors a system can produce. RGB and CMYK have different gamuts — they overlap, but neither fits entirely inside the other.

Key differences:

- RGB can produce vibrant colors CMYK can't: Bright, saturated colors — especially electric blues, neon greens, and vivid oranges — often look washed out when printed.

- CMYK can produce some colors RGB can't: Certain deep blues, rich browns, and muted pastels fall outside sRGB but are achievable with ink.

- Neither covers all visible colors: Both sRGB and CMYK are subsets of what the human eye can see.

#### How to Convert CMYK to RGB

There's no perfect formula because of the gamut differences and the many variables in printing (paper type, ink type, press quality). But there's a standard mathematical conversion that gives you a starting point:

##### The Standard Conversion Formula

Given C, M, Y, K values (each 0-1 or 0-100%):

- Convert percentages to 0-1 range (divide by 100)

- Calculate each RGB channel as: channel = 255 × (1 - c) × (1 - k)

- Where c is the CMY component for that channel (e.g., C affects R, M affects G, Y affects B)

More precisely:

R = 255 × (1 - C/100) × (1 - K/100)

G = 255 × (1 - M/100) × (1 - K/100)

B = 255 × (1 - Y/100) × (1 - K/100)

##### Example: Converting a Deep Blue

CMYK: C=100, M=80, Y=0, K=30

| Channel | Calculation | Value |

| Red | 255 × (1 - 1) × (1 - 0.3) = 255 × 0 × 0.7 | 0 |

| Green | 255 × (1 - 0.8) × (1 - 0.3) = 255 × 0.2 × 0.7 | ≈ 36 |

| Blue | 255 × (1 - 0) × (1 - 0.3) = 255 × 1 × 0.7 | ≈ 179 |

Result: rgb(0, 36, 179) or #0024B3

But remember — this is just a mathematical approximation. The actual printed color will look different depending on the printer, paper, and viewing conditions.

#### Why Your Prints Look Dull (And How to Fix It)

The #1 complaint from designers: "my prints look nothing like my screen." Here are the most common reasons and what to do about them:

##### 1. Your screen is too bright

Most monitors are set to 100% brightness out of the box, which is way too bright for design work. A properly calibrated monitor should be at 120 cd/m² — roughly the brightness of paper under office lighting.

##### 2. You're using sRGB for print

sRGB is the standard web color space and it's smaller than print gamut in some areas but larger in others. For print work, design in Adobe RGB or the specific CMYK profile of your printer (SWOP, FOGRA, etc.).

##### 3. No color management

Design software like Photoshop, Figma, and InDesign support color profiles. Use them. Set your document's color profile to match your printer's output profile — don't just trust the RGB preview.

##### 4. Paper matters more than you think

The same CMYK values look completely different on glossy photo paper vs matte vs newsprint. Glossy paper gives deeper blacks and more saturated colors. Newsprint absorbs ink and makes everything look muted.

⚠️ Proof before you print: Always ask for a printed proof before a large print run. Digital soft proofs (on-screen CMYK previews) help, but nothing beats seeing the actual ink on actual paper.

#### When to Use Which Format

| Use RGB / Hex When... | Use CMYK When... |

| Websites and web apps | Business cards and brochures |

| Social media graphics | Magazine and newspaper ads |

| Video and animation | Packaging and labels |

| Digital presentations | Billboards and large format prints |

| Email design | Books and book covers |

| Anything shown on a screen | Anything printed on physical material |

#### Spot Colors: When CMYK Isn't Enough

Sometimes you need an exact color that CMYK can't reproduce — like a specific brand red or a metallic gold. That's where spot colors (like Pantone colors) come in.

Spot colors are pre-mixed inks that print as a single color, rather than being mixed from CMYK halftone dots. They're more expensive (each spot color is a separate plate on the press) but give you exact, consistent color across different print runs and materials.

Most brands specify their primary logo color as a Pantone spot color, then provide CMYK and RGB approximations for other uses.

#### Quick Tool for Conversions

Need to convert CMYK to RGB (or any other color format)? Our Color Converter handles 8+ formats including CMYK, RGB, hex, HSL, HSV, and more. Paste any value and get all conversions instantly.

## The Complete Guide to Color Contrast & Accessibility | HexColor Pro Blog

URL: https://hexcolorpro.pages.dev/blog/contrast-accessibility-guide

### The Complete Guide to Color Contrast & Accessibility

WCAG standards explained, plus how to measure contrast and avoid common mistakes.

By Yao Xiangqian · Nov 7, 2026 · 10 min read

Accessible color design isn't just a nice-to-have — it's essential for creating products that work for everyone. About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency. Many more have low vision or read their phones in bright sunlight. Good contrast ensures your content is readable by all.

In this guide, we'll break down the WCAG standards, explain how contrast ratios work, and give you practical tips for designing accessible color schemes.

#### What is Contrast Ratio?

Contrast ratio measures the difference in luminance (brightness) between two colors, typically text and its background. The ratio ranges from 1:1 (same color, zero contrast) to 21:1 (pure white on pure black).

It's calculated using a formula based on relative luminance — how bright a color appears to the human eye. Green contributes most to perceived brightness, blue the least, which is why blue text on black can be hard to read even though the hue difference seems obvious.

#### WCAG Standards at a Glance

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) define two levels of contrast compliance:

| Element | AA (minimum) | AAA (enhanced) |

| Normal text | 4.5:1 | 7:1 |

| Large text (18pt+ / 14pt bold) | 3:1 | 4.5:1 |

| UI components & graphics | 3:1 | — |

💡 What's "large text"? In WCAG terms, large text is 18pt (24px) or larger, or 14pt (18.66px) and bold. Most body text falls under the "normal text" category and needs 4.5:1 minimum.

##### Why Aim for AA vs AAA?

WCAG AA is the legal baseline in many regions (EU's EN 301 549, US Section 508, Canada's AODA). AAA is a higher standard that's harder to meet — many brand colors simply can't reach 7:1 on white. For most products, AA compliance is the practical target, with AAA as a stretch goal for body text where possible.

#### Common Accessibility Mistakes

##### 1. Light Gray Text on White

This is the #1 culprit. Designers love "subtle" gray text for secondary info, but #999 on white is only about 2.8:1 — well below the 4.5:1 minimum. If you must use light gray, make sure it's truly decorative or non-essential. For important secondary text, use a darker gray like #666 or #555.

##### 2. Color as the Only Indicator

"The red button is delete, the green one is save" — that's a problem for color-blind users. Always pair color with another cue: iconography, text labels, patterns, or position. Error states should have an icon and message, not just a red border.

⚠️ Common mistake: Form validation that only shows a red border on error fields. Add an error icon or message too.

##### 3. Low-Contrast Hover States

Buttons look fine in their default state but the hover/active state drops contrast. Always test all interactive states — default, hover, active, focus, disabled — for contrast.

##### 4. Pure White Text on Bright Colors

White text on bright colors like #6366f1 (indigo) looks great but might fall short. Let's check: white (#ffffff) on indigo (#6366f1) has a contrast ratio of about 4.0:1 — close but below 4.5:1 for body text. For buttons and headlines (large text), it passes AA at 3:1. Just be aware of the distinction.

#### How to Check Contrast

There are several easy ways to test contrast ratios:

- Use our Contrast Checker — plug in any two colors and get an instant WCAG pass/fail result

- Browser DevTools — in Chrome DevTools, inspect text elements and the color picker shows contrast ratio

- Extensions — tools like axe DevTools or Wave can scan whole pages for contrast issues

- Grayscale test — convert your design to black and white. If it's hard to read in grayscale, the contrast is too low

🎯 Quick check: If you squint and can still read the text comfortably, the contrast is probably good. If you have to strain, it's too low.

#### Designing Accessible Color Palettes

##### Start with Value Contrast

Here's a trick: design your palette in grayscale first. Get the value relationships right — dark enough text, light enough backgrounds, clear hierarchy — then add color on top. If your design works in grayscale, it will pass contrast checks and be readable by everyone.

##### Use Darker Shades for Text

Your brand color might be a bright blue, but that doesn't mean text needs to be the same blue. Create a darker version of your brand color specifically for text links. It will still read as "your brand" but will be much more readable.

##### Test with Real Content

Contrast tools test pure color swatches against each other. Real-world factors like font rendering, anti-aliasing, and font weight affect readability too. Always test with actual text at actual sizes on actual screens.

##### Consider Color Blindness

Contrast ratio is about luminance, not color difference, so it already helps with many forms of color blindness. But you should also check that color-coded information doesn't rely on hue alone. Use tools like Coblis or Color Safe to simulate how your design looks to people with different types of color vision deficiency.

#### Accessible Dark Mode

Dark mode has its own accessibility challenges. Pure black (#000000) backgrounds with pure white (#ffffff) text have maximum contrast (21:1) but can cause eye strain and halation for some users, especially at night. A better approach:

- Use a dark gray like #0f172a or #18181b instead of pure black

- Use off-white text like #e2e8f0 instead of #ffffff

- Make sure body text still meets 4.5:1 (it will — #e2e8f0 on #0f172a is about 14:1)

- Reduce the number of saturated accent colors — they vibrate more on dark backgrounds

#### The Business Case for Accessibility

Beyond the ethical and legal reasons, accessible design is just good design. Better contrast means your content is more readable in all conditions — bright sunlight, low-quality screens, old monitors, glanceable moments. Designing for the edges improves the experience for everyone.

Ready to check your colors? Use our Color Contrast Checker to test any pair against WCAG standards.
